#2475. NFL Week 12 upset alert: Don't count out Patrick Mahomes, Fernando Mendoza and these underdogs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's fitting that this Week 12 slate coincides with the Thanksgiving holiday because it's going to feel like a five-course dinner.

Starting on Wednesday, the NFL will be front and center for five of the following six days. We kick things off with the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams, featuring the return of Micah Parsons. Then, we have games on Thanksgiving, Black Friday, our typical Sunday slate, and, of course, "Monday Night Football." If you're not thankful for that heavy dose of football, then I don't know what to tell you.

Naturally, there will be some twists and turns along the way as we embark on the marathon, which will almost certainly include an upset or two. Last week, we clued you in on the Philadelphia Eagles and New York Jets as underdogs that could pull off the outright upset, and they proved us right. Now, we'll look to Week 12, comb through this monstrous slate, and highlight five teams that could be on upset alert.

As is tradition, the Lions will be on our television this Thanksgiving. Surprisingly, when they kick off from Ford Field this holiday, they'll do so as a home underdog, currently laying 2.5 points to the rival Chicago Bears. The Lions are a perfect 5-0 at home this season, and Thursday's contest will be the first time in 2026 when they'll be a home dog. Historically, Detroit has done pretty well against the Bears, winning seven of their last eight games against them and outscoring them by 9.0 PPG over that stretch.

They're riding a four-game winning streak at home over the Bears, where they've averaged 36.8 points per game and 439.5 total yards per game. More recently, they've swept Chicago in each of the last two seasons, including last year against former offensive coordinator Ben Johnson. Over that stretch, Jared Goff has thrown 11 touchdowns and just one interception, while averaging 305.5 passing yards per game.

If they want to keep that pristine record, Detroit will once again have to look to Jahmyr Gibbs to help, and the star back does have an advantageous matchup against the Bears. Entering Week 12, Chicago is giving up 4.5 yards per carry this season, which is tied for the sixth-highest in the NFL. Gibbs has tallied at least 100 scrimmage yards in four straight games against the Bears.

If the Lions come anywhere close to these prior averages, they shouldn't be considered a home dog.

It's somehow flying under the radar, but Patrick Mahomes looks like he's back to full strength. Of course, the Chiefs quarterback has become a runaway favorite for Comeback Player of the Year after tearing his ACL and LCL last year and starting right out of the gate for Kansas City. That was impressive on its own. Now, Mahomes is not just setting himself up for the CPOY award, but he could even be making a late push for MVP. Over his last four games, Mahomes has been nothing short of dominant, totaling 13 touchdowns and zero interceptions.

Mahomes leveling up comes just in time for Kansas City's pivotal road matchup against the Bills to cap off the Thanksgiving slate. His stellar run will be put to the test, as the Bills' defense has not allowed a touchdown in 15 straight quarters heading into Week 12. That said, the competition that Buffalo has faced over this stellar run hasn't been that fierce. Mahomes is a different animal entirely.

Famously, Mahomes and Josh Allen are knotted at 5-5 against one another entering their 11th duel on Thursday night. Buffalo has seen all of their success against Mahomes come in the regular season, so this would be a rare victory for Kansas City. That said, the defense is playing well enough to possibly contain Allen and Co. just enough to help Mahomes edge out the victory. This season, Kansas City is tied for the third-fewest yards allowed per play (4.9) and has the best red zone defense in the NFL (36% touchdown rate).

The Seahawks are the more rested team heading into the NFC West matchup, an advantage that shouldn't be overlooked. Seattle was on the bye in Week 11, while the Niners were playing an international game in Mexico City against the Vikings. That alone should give the Seahawks a little bit of a leg up. However, the biggest reason to back them to possibly upset the 49ers is that they're the more desperate team.

Seattle enters Week 12 on the fringe of the playoff picture as the No. 8 seed. Depending on what happens during the Thanksgiving Eve contest between the Packers (the No. 7 seed) and Rams (the No. 9 seed), there could be a window for them to rise up in the standings. If they lose, their hopes of repeating as Super Bowl champs could start to slip away.

When these two faced one another back in Week 5, the 49ers rolled into Lumen Field and picked up a win. Sam Darnold, who is scheduled to make his return this week after missing two games with injury, wasn't his best in that contest. He completed 18-of-29 for 195 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. Despite that, Seattle hung around and nearly put themselves in an opportunity to go for the win or force overtime, but a controversial spot on a fourth-down completion to Cooper Kupp ended the game.

This time around, the Seahawks should get much better production from their rushing attack now that Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price are back in the fold. Without either of them in Week 5, they averaged 3.4 yards per carry as a team. If they can get more of a consistent ground attack, that'll only help Darnold in the passing game.

It hasn't been perfect, but I like what I've seen out of Fernando Mendoza over his first two starts. The No. 1 overall pick was put in a rough spot in his first two games as QB1, with home games against the Seattle Seahawks and then the Broncos in Denver. Last week he completed just 48.6% of his passes, but there were flashes as he also tossed for 267 yards and three touchdowns as he tried to keep Las Vegas in the game. He also didn't have Brock Bowers as the starting tight end, who was sidelined with an ankle injury. Cleveland gives up the same amount of yards per play (5.2) as the Broncos, so this will be another tough test for Mendoza on Sunday.

However, the Browns have almost exclusively been in one-score games. All six of their wins have been by four points or less, while eight of their 10 games have been decided by one score. With it constantly coming down to the wire, all Mendoza may need to do is make one or two special throws late, which he's more than capable of when accounting for his heroics at Indiana last year.

On top of being intrigued by Mendoza, I'm also curious to see if Ashton Jeanty can build off of arguably his best game of the season. Against Denver, Jeanty rushed for 79 yards and caught five of his eight targets for 90 yards and a touchdown. This season, the Browns are giving up 126.3 rushing yards per game, which is the ninth-highest in the NFL. Their 4.6 yards per carry allowed is tied for the fifth-highest. If Jeanty can take advantage of this matchup, that only makes things easier for Mendoza, who is eyeing his first career win as a starter.

For whatever reason, the Dolphins own the Jets. Miami is 1-9 on the season and that lone victory came back in Week 7 when they rolled up to East Rutherford and took down New York, 28-25. While Kyle McCord will now be at quarterback compared to Malik Willis, who started that game earlier this year, the Dolphins' success against the Jets goes beyond 2026.

They enter Week 12 on a 10-game winning streak at home against the Jets. Funny enough, the last road win the Jets had against the Dolphins came back in 2014 when ... Geno Smith was the quarterback. More recently, the Dolphins are 17-4 against the Jets since 2016, tied for the third-best record among division matchups over that span. Over the last two seasons, Miami is 3-0 against the Jets and 5-19 against every one else. That's the definition of having someone's number.

Moreover, Aaron Glenn hasn't proven that he can beat any division rival, as the Jets head coach is 0-9 in his career against the AFC East with a -16.8 PPG differential. He'd become the fourth head coach in NFL history to start a career 0-10 vs. divisional opponents. Until he proves otherwise, it's wise to roll with the trend and take the value with Miami.

#2474. NFL experts make Week 11 picks; LaMelo Ball driving Timberwolves' success; No. 1, No. 3 teams in Top 25 lose

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

The best part of writing the Thursday AM newsletter is knowing that we get to kick off a new week of NFL football while reading Pete Prisco's game-by-game predictions.

The Texans and Colts will get Week 11 started with an AFC South battle tonight, but let me take us to Philadelphia. The Steelers and Eagles meet in the battle of Pennsylvania, and both sides need a win. Pittsburgh just got blown out by the Bengals, and Philly has lost seven straight games.

Prisco likes the Steelers to get it done on the road, despite the Eagles coming off a bye.

Still, not all of our experts think the Steelrs will roll. Tyler Sullivan says Pittsburgh could be on upset alert in The Linc. In his complete Week 11 picks, Sullivan predicts a few blowouts.

The most highly anticipated matchup of the week features the Vikings taking on the 49ers. More specifically, the chess match between Kyle Shanahan and Brian Flores will be worth the price of admission.

When Anthony Edwards went down with injury just four games into the season, it seemed like the Timberwolves might be cooked. Instead, Minnesota is sitting at 11-4, fourth in the West and up to No. 3 in our latest NBA Power Rankings.

Much of that success is owed to LaMelo Ball, who is shining in his first season with the Wolves. He's averaging 17.7 points, 5.5 assists and 1.9 steals. For more evidence of Ball's impact, just look at how the team he left is doing without him. Brad Botkin explains:

Botkin: "The LaMelo effect is being felt in two places: Minnesota, of course, but also Charlotte, where the offense has plummeted from a 123.3 rating with Ball on the court last year to a league-worst 103.1 this season. Being down Kon Knueppel doesn't help, but it's night and day watching this unit try to generate clean looks without Ball's creation and passing."

#2473. Cubs signing NPB slugger Teruaki Sato on six-year, $120 million contract as offseason overhaul continues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not long after fortifying their rotation with the signing of Trevor Rogers, the Chicago Cubs have struck again by landing slugger Teruaki Soto out of Japan on a six-year, $120 million contract, ESPN reports.

Earlier in the offseason, CBS Sports ranked Sato, who turns 28 in March, as the No. 4 free agent of the current 2026-27 class. Here's part of our write-up:

"He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll."

Sato is expected to play a corner outfield spot for the Cubs even though he's a corner infielder by trade. He does, however, have significant time in the outfield, where the Cubs are in need of help after the incumbent corner outfielders, Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, departed in free agency. In 2026, Suzuki and Happ combined for a WAR of 7.8, so the bar for Sato will be relatively high when it comes to replacing a chunk of that value.

In addition to the $120 million contract owed to Sato, the Cubs also must pay Sato's former team, the Hanshin Tigers, a posting fee. For contracts in excess of $50 million, the posting agreement between MLB and NPB mandates that the posting fee will be 20% of the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the next $25 million plus 15% of the total guaranteed value exceeding $50 million. In the Cubs' case, that comes to a bit more than $20 million they'll owe Hanshin.

The Cubs are coming off a 2026 season in which they won 89 games and earned a postseason berth as the second-place team in the National League Central. In the playoffs, though, they were swept out of the Wild Card Series by the San Diego Padres in two games.

#2472. Victor Wembanyama takes hypocritical jab at 'stat-padding peers' after hunting his own 50-piece

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Victor Wembanyama is hard to put into words. Stephen Curry is the only player I can remember thinking of the same way in the post-Michael Jordan era. Nobody else. With Steph and Wemby, you can't fully describe what you've seen. You try, but in the end you just have to see them to understand. It's totally different than anything you've ever witnessed on a basketball court.

So here we go again, trying to write about the indescribable Wembanyama, who put 50 points, 19 boards, five blocks and four steals on the Pelicans on Saturday. It feels like we're qualifying one of his "first in history" stat lines about once a week, and indeed, Wembanyama is the first player since blocks and steals became an official stat in 1973 to record those single-game numbers.

Just take a look at this guy making the greatest basketball players in the world look like children.

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA BECOMES THE FIRST PLAYER SINCE 1973-74 TO RECORD 50+ PTS, 15+ REB, 4+ STL AND 5+ BLK IN A GAME!🤯 50 PTS🤯 18 REB🤯 5 BLK🤯 4 STL🤯 5 3PM🤯 32 MINSPURS WIN THEIR 14TH IN 15 GAMES. pic.twitter.com/lPKk3jYNjL

Before the halftime buzzer had even sounded, Wembanyama had already tallied 32 points, 13 rebounds, three steals and three blocks. That would be a career game for a lot of NBA players. He had played 18 minutes. You can only laugh at this point.

What was even funnier, however, was Wembanyama's comment after the game, when he took a clear stab at, well, whoever he considers his "peers" to be by calling them out for, shall we say, unethical statistical pursuits.

"It is very special," Wembanyama said of reaching the 50-point mark for the second time this season and third time in his career. "But unlike many of my peers, I'm not good at stat-padding. So I haven't reached it as many times as I should have."

Victor Wembanyama after scoring 50 points: “Unlike many of my peers, I'm not very good at statpadding.” pic.twitter.com/OAogFCa2oi

So here's what's interesting about this little dig: Wembanyama was definitely guilty of stat-padding his way to 50 in this game. With just more than eight minutes remaining and the Spurs up by 24, Wembanyama could've stayed on the bench after the timeout. The Spurs have made a concerted effort to limit his minutes whenever possible this year. Even in the golden age of comebacks, this game was over.

But Wemby stayed in and proceeded to take five straight shots on the next five possessions. He was hunting the 50. No question about it. He even admitted as much.

"The greats of the game, they don't care [about stat-padding]," Wemby said, via The Athletic. "I don't think Wilt [Chamberlain] thought about that when he had 98 points. ... That stepback 3, going right, that I took, it doesn't correlate with this. It didn't fit to the definition [of ethical basketball], for example. So I did try [to stat-pad] at the end."

Good on Wemby for acknowledging his own hypocrisy, but it raises the question: if you just did the very thing you are railing against, why take the jab in the first place? Every player who has been within range of 50 points has gone for it as long as it's not a competitive game in which quality shots still matter. It's not that big a deal.

But Wemby has done this before. In December of 2025, after the Spurs had just defeated the Thunder, he said, "I'm just glad to be part of something that's growing to be so beautiful — pure and ethical basketball."

This was a definite jab at Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's foul-baiting. Wemby, meanwhile, has turned into one of the more theatrical floppers in the league. In almost every way, Wembanyama is different than any other basketball player in the world. But when it comes to this ethical, non-stat-padding basketball soapbox he has climbed upon on numerous occasions, the truth is he's just like everyone else. So enough with the jabs.

#2471. It wouldn't shock me if ... for NFL Week 12: Colston Loveland feasts on Thanksgiving, Browns RB shines

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When it comes to the holidays, it's best to expect the unexpected. Rarely do things go smoothly when everyone convenes for Thanksgiving, so it's the right idea to lie back and simply roll with the punches as they come in. For instance, you have no idea what that weird uncle will say at the dinner table, nor can you guarantee the turkey won't be overcooked. It's bound to go off the rails in some capacity, but the one constant that you can lean on is that there will be football to help distract you from the madness, including the dog running outside with one of the turkey legs.

That said, even the NFL is unpredictable, so it's up to us to try and see the forest through the trees and anticipate what could be on the horizon. Below, we're going to highlight a handful of storylines/individual performances from Week 12 that may surprise some people, but not us.

All NFL odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook.

It was a modest day at the office for the entire Bears offense in Week 11, but they edged out a 21-13 win over the Saints. For his part, Colston Loveland was targeted just three times. The tight end hauled in all three passes for 29 yards, but did have a thunderous touchdown in the second quarter. That score should serve as the appetizer for a possible eye-popping performance from the Bears star pass catcher in Chicago's upcoming Thanksgiving matchup with the Detroit Lions.

This is the first of two matchups between these NFC North rivals this season, and first place in the division is hanging in the balance during this holiday contest. The Bears are a slight road favorite, and if they want to prove the oddsmakers right, featuring Loveland would go a long way in that endeavor.

In Week 18 of last season (the last time Loveland played the Lions), the then rookie delivered arguably the best game of his career. He caught 10 of his 13 targets for 91 yards and a touchdown. Those receptions are still his career high. This season, the Lions have been extremely susceptible to tight ends, allowing the most receiving yards (740) and receiving touchdowns (11) to the position in the NFL. They're also giving up the third-most receptions (68) to the position group this season.

This is a tasty matchup that Ben Johnson and company should look to exploit to come out of Thanksgiving thankful for their ninth win of the season.

Gambling angle to note: Colston Loveland's receiving yards prop for Week 12 is 54.5 (-109 to the Over). Loveland is +145 to score a touchdown.

The vibes surrounding the Rams have been off ever since they kicked off their season opener in Australia. A season marred by injury has seen this once-dubbed "superteam" enter its bye last week at 6-4, on the outside looking in on the playoff picture as the No. 9 seed. As they emerge from the break, however, there is an opportunity in front of them to climb back into the playoff picture, but they'll need a little help.

First and foremost, they'll need to take care of business during the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game where they host the Packers. Green Bay is currently clinging to the No. 7 seed in the NFL at 6-4 on the season. A mere win over the Packers on Wednesday would temporarily vault L.A. into the No. 7 seed. However, if they want to hold onto it coming out of Week 12 entirely, they'll need to hold their nose and root for the San Francisco 49ers to defeat the Seattle Seahawks at home.

That won't be a small feat as Seattle is coming off of its bye and the Niners are coming off an international game in Mexico City. That said, if San Francisco can fend off the defending champions, that'd create the necessary breathing room for the Rams to hold onto their spot in the playoff picture. If the Seahawks win, they'd draw even at 7-4 and retain the tiebreaker thanks to their superior divisional record. It's not an impossible needle to thread, but the Rams will need to get some help over the holiday weekend.

Gambling angle to note: The Rams are -104 to make the playoffs. A Rams-49ers moneyline parlay pays out +159.

A QB controversy has been brewing in the Pacific Northwest, specifically between Sam Darnold and Drew Lock. That talk about a QB controversy has been almost exclusively external, however, as the Seahawks have noted that Darnold -- who has missed the previous two games with rib and quad injuries -- will resume his role as QB1 when healthy. Head coach Mike Macdonald also noted that the team is optimistic that Darnold's return under center will come this week as they emerge from their bye and take on the San Francisco 49ers.

Darnold has been sidelined for essentially four games so far (injured himself on the opening drive of the season opener), so we've seen what the offense looks like with Drew Lock at the helm. He's led Seattle to four wins (3-0 as the starter), while completing 73.1% of his passes and a 125.6 passer rating. By the numbers, Lock has outplayed Darnold from what we've seen so far in 2026, thus bringing up the question of whether or not to keep Lock as the starter.

Again, Darnold will be the guy whenever he's ready to return, so there is no real controversy yet. However, if/when he returns this week, he might be set up for failure, as the 49ers are playing as well as any team in the NFL right now.

If Darnold struggles and the Seahawks lose to the Niners to drop them to 6-5, that chatter to slot in Lock as QB1 will likely reach a fever pitch, particularly with the division and wild card races starting to slip away from them.

I flagged this in my Cover 32 column for Week 11, but it's worth highlighting yet again. The Pittsburgh Steelers are dangerously close to seeing their season fall out from under them. They were 6-2 entering Week 9, and upon their return to the field, have looked nothing like the club that appeared destined to make the playoffs amid Aaron Rodgers' final season. Pittsburgh has dropped two straight games over the past two weeks, which now has them starting to fall down the wild card standings.

At 6-4, they're clinging to the No. 7 seed in the conference, which makes Friday's matchup at home against the Denver Broncos as close to a must-win as you'll find in Week 12. The Broncos are a 3-point road favorite in this game, so the oddsmakers are projecting Pittsburgh to fall to 6-5. If they do, they run dangerously close to falling out of the playoff picture entirely.

Temporarily, that'd happen if the New England Patriots go to Los Angeles and beat the Los Angeles Chargers. New England would draw even at 6-5 with Pittsburgh but they own the head-to-head tiebreaker thanks to a Week 2 win. Of course, the Patriots will be without Drake Maye (fractured fibula), but things might be evened out on the QB front as Justin Herbert is currently in concussion protocol coming out of Week 11. That possibly sets up a Tommy DeVito vs. DJ Uiagalelei matchup that is a true coin flip.

While the Patriots could oust them from a playoff spot for this weekend, the bigger long-term concern is the Houston Texans. They are hosting the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday and are 6.5-point favorites. The double whammy for Pittsburgh would be for them to lose on Friday, see the Patriots beat the Chargers to shoot them down to the No. 8 seed, and then the Texans beat the Ravens to push them to 5-6. That's set up a Week 13 matchup between Pittsburgh and Houston that could very well be the nail in the coffin for their season if they don't turn things around.

Gambling angle to note: A Texans, Patriots, Broncos moneyline parlay is +329.

It hasn't been the sophomore surge that folks hoped to see from Judkins this season, as the Browns back has struggled to be consistent. His 3.4 yards per carry average is a tick lower than his 3.6 yards per carry over his rookie season and is averaging just 47 rushing yards per game (59.1 yards per game in 14 games as a rookie in 2025). However, Cleveland's "Sunday Night Football" matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders set Judkins up with a true bounce-back opportunity.

The Raiders' run defense has been horrid so far in 2026. Coming into Week 12, Las Vegas is giving up the most rushing yards to running backs in the NFL this season (130.5 yards per game). Their 13 rushing touchdowns allowed are tied for the second-most in the league. The Raiders defense is coming off of a Week 11 loss to the Broncos, where rookie back Jonah Coleman steamrolled them for 111 yards on the ground and three rushing touchdowns.

As he enjoyed his bye week, Judkins was probably licking his chops seeing Coleman post those numbers, knowing full well that he'll get to face them this coming week. Judkins, a 2025 second-round pick, has rushed for at least 100 yards just once in his young career. Well, it wouldn't shock us if he not only notched his second-career game with 100 yards on the ground, but surpassed his 110-yard rushing game from Week 5 last season for a new career-best mark. The Raiders have allowed a 100-yard rusher three times this season already.

#2470. Inter Milan U19: Team Analysis – MH

von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

Inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

Inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

To build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

The primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

If only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be quickly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

To effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

Through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

Even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

This three-man buildup creates new passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

Due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

Additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

The follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

One of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

While striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

The pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

Another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

Depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

Once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

Especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

As the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

Inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

In possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. We get to see two of the great players of their generation face off tonight in Edmonton's Connor McDavid and Tampa Bay's Nikita Kucherov. McDavid has won just about every major NHL award in his career possible – even a Conn Smythe Trophy in 2024 as playoff MVP despite the Oilers losing in seven to the Florida Panthers in the Finals.

McDavid is the massive -400 favorite to win a fourth career Hart Trophy as regular-season MVP after getting two more points Tuesday in a 5-2 win at Florida. It was the Oilers' sixth straight win as they improved to an astonishing 10-0-1 on the road. That shootout loss came in New Jersey back on Nov. 3. Edmonton is only the fifth team in NHL history to record 10 road wins in a single season in 11 games or fewer. The last do to it was the 2023-24 Los Angeles Kings.

It's rare to see such a big MVP favorite in November, but McDavid has a 23-game point streak to open the season, tied with Wayne Gretzky for the fourth-longest in NHL history. Gretzky (51 and 30), Mats Sundin (30) and Mario Lemieux (28) are the only players with longer streaks. McDavid leads the league by a mile with 55 points and has 28 in 11 road games. That 2.54-point-per-game road average has McDavid on pace for 106 road points, which would pass Gretzky (104 in 1985-86 and 1984-85) for the most in a single campaign.

Keep in mind that the NHL switched from an 82-game to 84-game regular season this year. Gretzky is the only player to have 200 points in a season and did it four times: 215 points in 1985-86, 212 in '81-82, 208 in '84-85 and 205 in '83-84. McDavid is on pace for 202.4 points. That he reaches 200, which I highly doubt, is +2200 and that he breaks Gretzky's mark of 215 is +10000.

Let's not forget about McDavid's unbelievable wingman Leon Draisaitl, who is second in the league with 44 points and tied for first with 21 goals. He had an assist Tuesday to extend a points streak to 10 games for the 12th time in his Hall of Fame career. That's tied with Peter Stastny for the second-most by a player born outside North America, behind Kucherov (13).

McDavid and Draisaitl can become the first set of teammates with 100 combined points through 24 games of a season since Penguins legends Lemieux and Jaromir Jagr (108) in 1995-96. McDavid is an absurd -425 for a point tonight, while Draisaitl is the game's +125 anytime goalscoring favorite.

#2468. Snyder's Soapbox: Until MLB owners open the books, there's no reason to listen to pleas of poverty

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Welcome to Snyder's Soapbox! Here, I pontificate about matters related to Major League Baseball on a weekly basis. Some of the topics will be pressing matters, some might seem insignificant in the grand scheme of things, and most will be somewhere in between. The good thing about this website is that it's free, and you are allowed to click away. If you stay, you'll get smarter, though. That's a money-back guarantee. Let's get to it.

The world of Major League Baseball -- which includes fans and media, too -- has something rather heavy hanging over its head this offseason. Obviously. We know all about that pesky CBA expiration on Dec. 1 and we know that the owners are all but certain to lock the players out that night while they push for a salary cap in the name of parity.

People are going to take sides, and I make no apologies for being firmly on the players' side. They are the talent and why we watch the games. No one is buying owners' jerseys and sitting in the ballpark facing the suites.

Another reason I'm not a huge fan, in general, of the owners is that I don't believe we're ever getting the full truth about how much money they make. The Braves are publicly traded and we can see a good breakdown of how they fared in 2025. The short version is that they are swimming in money. We could look at the two recently sold MLB teams for a hint, too. The Angels were sold for $4 billion; Arte Moreno bought the team for $184 million in 2003. The Padres were also sold recently for $3.9 billion. The San Diego media market size ranks ahead of only Kansas City, Cincinnati, Milwaukee and, eventually, Las Vegas among MLB cities.

And, again, sometimes you'll have an owner say the quiet part out loud. Enter Orioles owner David Rubenstein:

"A lot of my friends were buying teams, and I realized they're making money. They're making more money than I'm making in private equity," Rubenstein said last month at a forum with other pro sports owners at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C.

" ... I couldn't figure out why it is that people who are fans are so obsessed with the success of their local team. They're not going to make any more money. They're not going to go to the Super Bowl and get a trophy out of it."

People who cape for the owners: this is what you are defending.

Obviously every owner shouldn't be painted with the same brush. Some of them are legitimately fans. But I'd be willing to wager pretty heavily that a majority of the owners think like Rubenstein here and view the teams simply as vehicles to make as much money as possible.

Do we even need to bother with the suggestion that we shouldn't care about our favorite teams since they don't make us money and we don't get pieces of metal trophies? Sports fandom can be one of the purest and most wholesome things about our society. It brings families and friends together. It gives us emotions we otherwise couldn't even possibly imagine feeling. And I'll say this, too: I've seen my favorite team win the World Series and the absolute last thing on my mind was, "man, I'd sure like a trophy for my own mantle." The memories can't be matched by anything material at all. I would take nothing of real, tangible substance over those memories.

It's maddening that an owner can be so out of touch with the product that he purchased.

Do please hone in on the money comment, though. That's a much bigger deal. We've heard owners of some smaller-market teams cry poor for years and even decades, and the response from the MLBPA every single time is a pretty simple one. I reached out to a source and heard it again: "If any team wants us to believe they are losing money, they can simply open their books."

Yes. The Braves have to and we can see how much of a money machine they are in the 11th-ranked media market (counting the two-team cities twice).

Again, there will be exceptions, but the owners generally just view their teams as virtual ATMs, the output of which would be even higher with artificially decreased payroll because of a salary cap. At least one of them doesn't even understand why we care as much as we do.

#2467. 6 lessons from Week 11: Kyle Shanahan is as good as it gets, plus a rookie RB earning a role

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When I think about Thanksgiving, I think about going to my grandparents' house growing up. We'd leave immediately after my dad got off work on Wednesday and drive from my hometown in rural Virginia to my mom's parents in New Jersey. A quick stop at the McDonald's was the only time we'd leave our route. We'd drive extra miles to avoid traffic. I'd try, often unsuccessfully, to fight off sleep on the drive up.

Around midnight — sometimes later — we'd arrive at my grandparents' doorstep, weary but happy. They'd always greet us with smiling faces, no matter the hour.

And then there was Thanksgiving Day, which meant football. My grandpa, a die-hard Giants fan, would lead our collective yelling at the TV, hoping the Cowboys would lose, and we'd pity-root for the Lions, who seemingly never won.

The results fade, but what I remember is my family being together. It wasn't perfect. It got harder as my grandparents got older. We'd laugh, we'd cheer, we'd wish it could last forever.

It's been several years since then, but I still remember my grandparents waving us goodbye, my grandpa good-heartedly reminding my dad to go south, not north, on the turnpike. It felt like just minutes earlier, they had been standing in that doorway welcoming us in. It always went too fast.

So ahead of our six lessons, let me give you a non-football one: Try to cherish this week. If you can do it with family, great. If you can do it with friends, great. If all you can do is call or text, great. It doesn't have to be perfect. Whether you watch every football game this week or none at all, I hope you're surrounded by people you love.

Coach of the Year has become so misconstrued, and not just in the NFL. Every individual player award honors the best player, but for some reason Coach of the Year honors the coach whose team exceeds expectations most.

So, once again, Kyle Shanahan's magnificent job will likely go unrewarded, simply because he's done too good a job for too long. An early congratulations to either John Harbaugh or Todd Monken for winning. They've done magnificent jobs.

But Kyle Shanahan is the best coach in the NFL this season. The 49ers just dismantled the Vikings to move to 9-1. They have won games in Australia and Mexico and Seattle and Dallas, all places with their own unique challenges. They have won games using wide receivers they never imagined having to count on.

Thought you saw the best of Brock Purdy? Think again. I've written at length about why Purdy deserves MVP and is much more than just a product of the Shanahan system, but there's no doubt Shanahan has raised his game immensely. This offense is so well-constructed, so prepared for each and every task each and every week and so connected.

The Vikings love to blitz. Purdy shredded them with quick passes: 12-for-13 for 161 yards and two touchdowns on throws released in 2.5 seconds or faster. Minnesota entered the night leading the NFL in sack rate and pressure rate. It managed just one sack and a 29% pressure rate, both season lows.

Oh yeah, and Shanahan also made the excellent hire of defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, who has helped turn this defense from quite poor to elite.

It's silly that we'll look back and likely see someone else win Coach of the Year. Shanahan has never won the award, by the way, even though he's been the best or among the best in the profession for nearly a decade. Andy Reid, who's fourth all-time in wins, has won it once, back in 2002 with the Eagles. Sean McVay has won it once since becoming a head coach in 2017. Kevin Stefanski, a perfectly solid coach but nothing more, has won it twice.

Again, even if he doesn't win "Coach of the Year," Shanahan is very much the defining coach of this year. He'd gladly take a Lombardi Trophy over any individual award, anyway.

One day after Brian Flores' normally excellent defense was shredded, one of his disciplines had his best performance yet. Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones and his unit were terrific in a 22-20 upset win over the Bengals.

Jones, like Flores, brings extra pressure, big time. Washington is third in blitz rate this year. Joe Burrow has destroyed blitzes all year, but on Monday night, not so much.

Jones was without his best cornerback, Amik Robertson, but refused to back down. His corners played physically, aggressively and well. The safeties followed in kind. And while Cincinnati's running game has never been a strength, Washington turned it into a decided weakness. The Bengals' 14% rushing success rate was the worst by any team in any game this year.

Jones has this defense moving in the right direction, too. In November, the Commanders rank 15th in defensive EPA per play; they were 23rd before that. They've done a good job stopping the run and limiting explosives, largely because they have the third-lowest missed tackle rate in the league. Washington hasn't allowed more than 23 points in a game since Week 5.

There will be big-picture coaching questions in Washington if the team doesn't make the playoffs, but Jones has done solid work under the radar.

I wrote about this in our Week 11 overreactions, but the Steelers are once again a team with a winning record and little chance of winning a playoff game. Here, though, let's talk about the style.

Aaron Rodgers is now completing 21.6% of his passes thrown 20+ yards downfield. While he is throwing way more of them this year — only Jordan Love has more than Rodgers' 51 attempts — they're mostly performative "See? I'll still take shots downfield" throws that are low-percentage floaters. Only Cam Ward and recently released Daniel Jones have a lower completion rate on these throws.

The run game can be quite good. In fact, the Steelers are second in rushing EPA per play this year at 0.06. Earlier in the season, it seemed they finally had one truly sterling offensive aspect. This made them different.

But when the run game isn't going well, as has been the case the last two weeks, Pittsburgh has nothing else. The Steelers are 4-0 when their EPA per rush is above their overall season mark and 2-4 when it is below it. Pittsburgh was at -0.19, second-worst of the season, in the Week 11 loss to the Eagles.

The Steelers have been the same as they've been during this playoff win drought: poor quarterbacking, good-not-great defense.

Just a dull, stuck-going-nowhere team archetype and a franchise that seems fine with it.

The Chiefs' three-game winning streak has coincided with a soft schedule. There's not a ton to take away from it in terms of Kansas City's standing in the championship-contending pecking order.

But on an individual level, Emmett Johnson is a beast. In his two starts with Kenneth Walker III out, Johnson has 134 yards from scrimmage and three touchdowns.

Emmett Johnson has now recorded back to back 100 yard rushing games since taking over for Kenneth Walker.23 CAR, 105 RUSH YDS, 1 TD, 4 REC, 38 REC YDS vs Cardinals.Johnson's OROY chances have skyrocketed over the last two weeks. https://t.co/dt5FdKVwLi pic.twitter.com/tNep8zsuxb

Johnson currently leads all running backs in 7.0 yards per touch (min. 50 touches). He also leads all running backs in tackle avoidance rate (36.8), which is also first and slightly higher than tackle-avoiding machine Walker III.

Johnson has a true three-down skill set. Only 11.3% of his rushes go for 0 or negative yards, the fourth-lowest rate among all running backs with at least 50 touches, and he has turned several potential losses into gains.

Walker is a stud. He'll be the feature back when he returns from his groin injury. But Johnson has proved he not only deserves a legit complementary role down the stretch and beyond, but with his pass-catching acumen, he can actually be a weapon, too.

The Colts got thumped 26-3 by the Texans on Thursday, and that somehow wasn't the worst aspect of their week. Not even close.

One day after that, Indianapolis released Daniel Jones, and shortly after that, reports surfaced that at the trade deadline, the Colts had turned down the Ravens' offer of a fourth-and fifth-round pick for Jones (the fifth would be returned if Baltimore made the playoffs). Now, they get nothing for Jones and will carry a $35.2 million dead cap hit in 2027.

If interim GM Ed Dodds wasn't already filling in for a fired GM (Chris Ballard), this would be a fireable offense. Maybe it is, anyway. The Colts sold away many of their franchise pillars but stopped at Daniel Jones?

According to various reports, the Colts turned away multiple suitors for Jones, including Baltimore's potentially lucrative one; multiple suitors for Jonathan Taylor, who fetched offers for a second-round pick plus more; at least one offer that included a fourth-round pick for veteran defensive tackle Grover Stewart, who's 33 and in a contract year.

I gave the Colts a D+ in my trade deadline grades and, upon first reflection, thought I might have been a little harsh. Indianapolis did get decent draft capital back for the moves it did make. But now, I think that mark might be generous. Every meaningless hard hit Taylor takes, and every meaningless double-team Stewart takes on, is just that. Meaningless.

The Colts have very little young, cost-controlled talent. They don't have their first-round pick in 2027. They will have a new GM and, likely, a new coach. They are arguably the worst team in the NFL in 2026. They will be in the running for worst team in the NFL in 2027 and potentially 2028. They just turned down draft capital for a player they didn't even want. If there were a class in mismanaging an enterprise worth billions of dollars, the Colts' front office could do a great job teaching it.

If it feels like there's been a little bit of a midseason lull, it's because there has been. In November, there's been a ton of blowouts — seven games decided by 15+ every week from Week 8-10, and then a lot of byes and semi-competitive games in Week 11.

But the league is cranking it up a notch this coming week.

The Bears have won five straight, but their last two are over the lowly Buccaneers and Saints, with a bye in between. The Lions have won six straight, but the last three are over the Dolphins, the Patriots (mostly without Drake Maye) and the Buccaneers. I'm a huge believer in "you can only beat who's on your schedule." But in terms of learning about these teams, the past few weeks haven't been very helpful.

That all changes this week. On Thanksgiving, the 8-2 Lions host the 8-2 Bears (on CBS and streaming on Paramount+, by the way!), which should be an absolute banger.

This is far from the only example. Get your nap in early, because later that night, Chiefs at Bills is a can't-miss. Buffalo has seemed almost bored — and certainly hasn't been very sharp — in wins over the Ravens, Carson Wentz-led Vikings, Jets and Dolphins. But they'll absolutely be locked in against their bitter rival. The Chiefs, meanwhile, have cruised past the Jets, Falcons and Saints after a tough loss to the Broncos. We have questions about Josh Allen's turnovers, Patrick Mahomes' deep-passing renaissance — is it real or fake? — and much more.

#2466. Ranking NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Knicks hit their stride, while Celtics take step back

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Let's call the last seven days the NBA's first parity week of the season. Take a look at the standings right now. The No. 2 through the No. 6 seeds in the Eastern Conference standings all have exactly six losses, and while the Philadelphia 76ers hold a three-game lead for the No. 1 seed, they've done so behind a preposterous 12-0 clutch record. When they regress to the mean, we seem destined for an Eastern Conference packed like sardines.

The Western Conference is similarly crunched. The San Antonio Spurs and Los Angeles Lakers sit atop the standings with identical 14-3 records... but seeds 3-9 are all separated by no more than two games. Even the Sacramento Kings got a win this week! The NBA has spent years tinkering in order to create parity, and right now, at least it's getting it. With that unofficial week of parity in the books, let's crown some winners and losers from the last seven days.

You're expecting me to talk about Wemby's 50-point, 18-rebound, five-block, four-steal performance against the New Orleans Pelicans, aren't you? That'd be the easy starting point. We could just as easily kick things off with Luka Dončić's shooting dip, as he has quietly shot roughly 41-31-82 in his past five games, bringing his ridiculous offensive numbers down to slightly more mortal levels and making Wembanyama, for now, the slight MVP betting favorite. Totally reasonable. They're both contributors to his excellent week.

Neither stands up to what Wembanyama did against the Los Angeles Clippers on Thursday. He shunked. That's a word that didn't exist when we woke up on Thursday. It is now, hilariously, a signature moment of Wembanyama's young career. He has apparently dunked so often, so violently that he suffered a hand injury that compelled him to try, and succeed, to shoot a jump shot at the rim.

Did Wemby just... shoot it from above the rim??? 🤯😲 pic.twitter.com/1YDxy8mwy8

The MVP race is for the season. The ridiculous numbers are for the history books. The shunk wins the week. Any time you suffer and overcome a dunking-related injury by inventing a new form of scoring, you win the week.

The champs have won five in a row and are 11-3 overall since their 0-3 start, but this isn't as simple as the Knicks suddenly looking like the Knicks again. Many of the early season problems are still persisting. Mikal Bridges hit the game-winner on Friday and still shot 3-of-12 on Sunday. Josh Hart missed all four of his 3-pointers on Sunday and is below 26% shooting from deep so far this season. The starters, as a group, are still getting outscored by almost 13 points per 100 possessions after struggling mightily in the past two regular seasons.

Yet they just keep winning. There are obvious basketball reasons for that. Karl-Anthony Towns is getting every rebound, making every shot, and has readopted the playmaking hub role he thrived in throughout the postseason, particularly when it comes to assisting Jalen Brunson. The bench is thriving. Landry Shamet is shooting better than 45% on 3s and Deuce McBride isn't far behind. Tyler Kolek has a 61-to-9 assist-to-turnover ratio.

But there's something deeper here, a resilience and versatility that developed over last season's championship run that is sustaining thus far this season. OG Anunoby has missed the past two games. Towns missed the Blazers game. Bridges and Hart play most of some games and only parts of others because of their early season struggles. Yet Mike Brown just keeps pulling the right levers, and the Knicks just keep figuring it out. Championships can bring about this certainty. The Knicks aren't quite themselves yet, but they have an internalized confidence that came from dominating the playoff crucible a year ago that's paying off handsomely right now.

It's hard to tell what we've seen from the Heat thus far this season that really deserves scrutiny. They started 0-4 in part because opponents weren't missing any 3s. They've gone 8-2 since, but they haven't beaten a single notable, fully healthy opponent during their active seven-game winning streak. No Evan Mobley against the Cleveland Cavaliers. No Jalen Duren against the Detroit Pistons. No Amen Thompson against the Houston Rockets. No... basically anyone against the Oklahoma City Thunder on Sunday, though in fairness, Giannis Antetokounmpo missed that game himself. Miami is something of a Rorschach test so far. You're going to see what you're predisposed to seeing.

But if we're going to panic during the shooting luck-induced losing streak, we're going to have to acknowledge the positives during the winning streak. The maligned Heat offense ranks in the top five over their past 10 games largely because Klay Thompson is shooting like Klay Thompson again and Giannis Antetokounmpo never stopped dunking like Giannis Antetokounmpo. Their core lineups featuring Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo are deterring rim attempts and giving up basically no corner 3s. Andrew Wiggins looks more like Andrew Wiggins since moving to the bench. As tempted as I was to give the third slot to the player development coaches for the Memphis Grizzlies after Cam Spencer's breakout 26-point game against Cleveland, the seven-game Miami winning streak gets the nod.

The Celtics were too clever by a half with their lineup decisions this weekend. They sat Jayson Tatum and Derrick White against the hapless Kings and then sat Paul George in the second half of that back-to-back against the Stephen Curry-less Golden State Warriors. They lost both very winnable games by a single point when they probably could have ensured a split and maybe even a sweep by aligning the rest. Throw in a 17-point blown lead to the Denver Nuggets and allowing a 40-point fourth quarter against the Orlando Magic and the previously 11-2 Celtics lost all four of their games this week. They're back with the Eastern Conference pack.

It's too early to draw any real conclusions, just as it was too early to crown them Eastern Conference favorites when they were throttling the Sixers two weeks ago, but this week was a reminder of some of the cracks here. Their best player is coming off of a torn Achilles, and their second- and third-best players are in their 30s and have to be managed carefully throughout the season. You can get away with never getting to the basket as a team when you're an elite 3-point shooting outfit. The Celtics haven't been this season, and we're now in Year 2 of Derrick White's 3-point drought (and, for that matter, arguably Year 3 of Jayson Tatum's). Mitchell Robinson will put together a few good stretches and then regress back into the mess he's been for most of the season. Boston has been nearly 22 points stronger per 100 possessions with him off the floor this season.

The Celtics, given their playing style and roster makeup, are vulnerable to the ebbs and flows of an 82-game season. When everyone's available and they're making their shots, they're going to look unbeatable. This week is what happens when they're not, and considering how frequently that's been the case for them in the playoffs, it's something the Celtics are going to have to learn to play through if they hope to make it through this crowded East.

Slowly but surely, the NBA's cellar dwellers are starting to come around. The Utah Jazz won twice this week. The Chicago Bulls have won three times since Caleb Wilson went down, and they pushed the Denver Nuggets to overtime on Sunday. The Kings got win No. 2 on Saturday, but also pushed the Los Angeles Lakers to the brink on Friday. There is still a whole lot of misery at the bottom of the standings, but all of these teams can find small pockets of optimism.

Not the Bucks, who are now the NBA's last one-win team and owners of a 13-game losing streak. One of those losses came against Miami this week as their former franchise player, Antetokounmpo, throttled them for three quarters before they made the final score look respectable in the fourth quarter. They have the NBA's worst defense comfortably. Beyond a three-game stretch in which second-year guard Kasparas Jakučionis averaged 21 points per game, it's simply been a miserable season in Milwaukee, and it's one that could get worse any day now as the NBA investigates potential salary cap circumvention involving Gary Trent Jr. We all knew the Bucks would struggle with post-Giannis life, but this is worse than anyone could have imagined.

Tyrese Haliburton has played four games this season at a roughly All-Star level. The Indiana Pacers are now 3-10 in all other contests, and ESPN reported Friday that Haliburton is set to miss at least another few weeks with a left hamstring strain. This is after a 19-win season played entirely without Haliburton a year ago. At this point, obvious as it sounds, it's simply become clear that the Pacers can't win consistently without their best player. That was obvious in a playoff context, but the regular-season implications here are starting to add up.

Indiana is already six games out of a top-six Eastern Conference seed. Even when Haliburton gets back, he's probably not going to be perfectly healthy for the entire rest of the season just given his own history of durability concerns. The East's bottom four teams are thankfully so dreadful that there's probably a floor of No. 11 here, but Indiana will eventually have to pass someone -- presumably the Washington Wizards, perhaps someone else who gets bitten by the injury bug -- just to make it back into the Play-In Tournament picture. Even if they're there, their road to and through the playoffs becomes enormously precarious. It doesn't matter how dangerous you are in a playoff setting if you can't actually survive the regular season and make it there. It's too early to say that's where Indiana is headed, but the danger is very real.

#2465. Dylan Larkin trade grades: Red Wings notch massive win in blockbuster NHL deal with Canadiens

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Detroit Red Wings have traded former captain Dylan Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a blockbuster trade, the teams announced on Sunday. This deal ends a bitter saga between Larkin and the Red Wings, and Montreal gave up a king's ransom to make it happen.

In addition to Larkin, Detroit sent a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Montreal. The Red Wings received forward Kirby Dach, goaltender Sam Montembeault, prospect Michael Hage, first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fourth-round pick.

Larkin requested a trade back in June, and his relationship with the Red Wings only grew more acrimonious with each passing day. As training camp opened in September, Detroit announced that Larkin had been stripped of his captaincy, and Larkin was booed by fans on opening night at Little Caesars Arena.

After recovering from an injury he suffered in camp, Larkin played 10 games before announcing that he would be sitting out in anticipation of the trade. While sitting out, Larkin racked up major fines, but his trade request has finally been granted.

When he's on the ice, there's no denying that Larkin can make a significant impact. The 30-year-old Larkin just notched 34 goals and 33 assists for the Red Wings last season -- his fifth straight year hitting the 30-goal mark -- and he was instrumental in Team USA ending its lengthy gold medal drought at the 2026 Olympics.

In his career, Larkin has totaled 278 goals and 371 assists in 818 games. The first game Larkin — a native of Waterford, Michigan — plays for the Habs will also be the first he's ever played for a team based outside the Wolverine State.

Larkin will give the Canadiens much-needed center depth, and he'll be under contract for a while. He's in the fourth year of an eight-year contract that pays him $8.7 million per season.

This trade fills a void that's existed in the Canadiens' lineup for several years now. Nick Suzuki has evolved into a legitimate star and a franchise-caliber No. 1 center. Beyond him, Montreal has struggled to find a true second-line center.

Larkin absolutely fits that bill. While he was a bit miscast in Detroit as a first-line center, Larkin is one of the best No. 2 options in the NHL, and he gives the Canadiens an elite one-two punch down the middle.

Did the Canadiens overpay a bit for a 30-year-old second-line center? In a vacuum, they did. However, taken in context, this deal makes plenty of sense for the Habs.

Montreal's championship window is just now opening. It already has an elite young core locked up for the next several seasons on team-friendly deals. Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Ivan Demidov, Juraj Slafkovsky, Lane Hutson and Noah Dobson are all 27 or younger and make less than $10 million per season.

That gives general manager Kent Hughes a bit more freedom to be aggressive on the trade market. Picks and prospects are nice, but they don't do much good for a team looking to make the jump to contender status in 2026-27. Besides, the Canadiens have been building their prospect pool for years now. It's time to flip some of those assets for proven star power.

The Canadiens paid a premium to acquire Larkin. There's no two ways about it. However, Montreal fills a major need and looks a lot more formidable in the Eastern Conference. The Stanley Cup window is officially wide open for the ascending Canadiens. Grade -- B+

Consider the situation interim general manager Shawn Horcoff faced. Everyone knew that Larkin wanted out of Detroit so badly that he was paying not to play for the Red Wings.

On top of that, Larkin had a full no-trade clause, and his list of approved teams amounted to no more than a dozen.

Should I also mention that Horcoff was thrust into this role in the midst of the offseason, when franchise legend Steve Yzerman was effectively fired for mishandling the Wings' rebuild?

Given all of that, it's hard to see this as anything less than a home run for Detroit. In fact, it's probably more like a grand slam. Not only did the Red Wings get multiple first-round picks and a couple useful NHL players out of the deal, but they also landed a legitimate blue-chip prospect in Hage.

The No. 21 pick in the 2024 NHL Draft, Hage is off to a roaring start at the University of Michigan this season with five goals and 21 assists in just 13 games. Detroit might have replaced one franchise center with another one, assuming Hage continues to develop at this rate.

This was a great piece of work from Horcoff, who probably just made a strong case for the full-time general manager gig in Detroit. This haul will allow the Wings to kickstart another retool or swing a big trade to bolster the current roster. Either way, the outlook just got a lot brighter in Hockeytown. Grade -- A+
